## Findings by module

### 5

- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Murch on why cuts work and the practice that follows: each frame is a small displacement that the eye reads as motion, while a cut is a larger displacement that the mind must re-evaluate as a new context. Cutting needs a motivated change of view, so a cut from a full shot to a slightly tighter one is too small to read as a change. Discontinuity lets the editor choose the best angle for each emotion. Core reason for the course's coverage and cut-size rules.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Murch's shooting-ratio figures (about 95 unseen minutes per minute on Apocalypse Now, against about 20:1 for a typical feature) and his 'shadow splices' (about fifteen tried and lifted for every splice kept). Use as the reason to plan coverage and to expect most work to be discarding.
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): Murch's rules of thumb for the course's editing section: always try to do the most with the least; suggestion beats exposition; do not cut just because you can; 'cut out the bad bits' is the editor's real job; and the Rule of Six (emotion, story, rhythm, eye-trace, two-dimensional plane, three-dimensional space, in that order) is the criterion for a cut. Chapter 3 is the source for these; quote no more than fifteen words.
- **extended** (ch-005.txt): Murch's practice of a still photo for each setup from the workprint: a representative frame (the 'decisive moment') gives the crew a record of hairline, costume and colour, and a sheet of them lets the editor read a scene's emotional arc at a glance. Useful for the course's continuity and camera-report workflow.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Murch on why a cut works, the blink: a blink marks the point where a viewer separates one thought from the next, and a cut placed at the moment the mind has 'got' an idea reads as a punctuation mark rather than a jump. A cut should land where the blink would, not a frame before or after. Useful for the course's 'cut on the thought' note.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Murch's pacing numbers for the course's editing section, as he gives them: real blinking runs about 4 to 40 a minute; an action sequence can carry about 25 cuts a minute and a dialogue scene about 6 (American features of his time). Choose branch points by the thought the audience is having. He calls the 'Dragnet' rule (cut to every speaker) shallow. Attribute as Murch's figures.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Murch's Rule of Six weights (his own, offered as rough): emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, eye-trace 7%, two-dimensional plane 5%, three-dimensional space 4%. He says sacrifice from the bottom up. Present as Murch's ordering for judgement, not as measured percentages.
- **note** (ch-003.txt): Murch on misdirection and on seeing only the screen: an editor should watch the finished image as the audience will (a mural, not a miniature), and keep the shooting's surplus out of the cut. Useful for the course's note that the editor is the audience's ombudsman.
- **note** (ch-004.txt): Murch's director-editor relation: the editor proposes alternates as bait so the film's own 'dream' reveals what it needs; roles swap as the cut goes on. Practical note: a crew of two editors speeds the work at a cost to coherence (his Godfather history). Use as the course's note on working with a director at the edit.
- **note** (ch-006.txt): Murch's test-screening advice: trust what the audience shows you (where the pain is), not what they say the cause is (referred pain); test after a day or two; and at the last stage a change becomes permanent, so make the case in private first. Useful for the course's note on previews.
- **note** (ch-008.txt): Murch's 'galaxy of winking dots': if an audience is in the film, its blinks cohere (nobody coughs at key moments); an infrared check would show when attention drifts. The same test explains why a nervous or inattentive actor's blink rhythm seems wrong. Use as a metaphor for the audience's attention; it is Murch's idea, not a measured finding.
- **note** (ch-009.txt): Murch's cut-count examples (cuts in the first twenty minutes): Sunset Boulevard about 85; The Third Man about 225; The Sixth Sense about 170; Fight Club about 375 in its last twenty. Use as examples of how pace has moved over time, attributed to Murch's count.
- **note** (ch-009.txt): Murch on digital speed: linear flatbeds show every frame at high speed (each on screen for about a 240th of a second), while digital random-access systems skip frames to play fast, so fast review can hide a cut. He also gives four habits for digital work: highest resolution affordable, screen the 35mm workprint, conform early, and test on a large screen; and the 'miniature vs mural' check with two paper figures. Practical for the course's digital workflow.
- **note** (ch-009.txt): Murch's afterword (2001): digital editing is now standard, with the Avid in most use; the random-access advantage needs good notes and the linear system's full-frame review is lost; and the reasons he gives for cinema's staying power (shared human need for stories in the dark, collaboration). Useful as a note for the course's digital-workflow module; treat the forecasts as opinion.

### 2

- **note** (ch-005.txt): Murch on colour checks at the edit: judge workprint against the answer print on a light box of the right colour temperature, because a bright screen hides a slight green or blue cast. Practical, and it matches the course's colour-balance notes.
